body.p: The Office Action dated March 28, 2024 ("Office Action") has been carefully reviewed and these remarks are responsive thereto. No new matter has been added. Claims 1-20 remain pending in this application. Reconsideration and allowance of the present application are respectfully requested.

Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 because the claimed invention is allegedly directed to an abstract idea without significantly more. In particular, the Office Action alleges that the claims are directed to the abstract ideas of "processing data according to the rules of a game," "displaying the output," and "accepting input." See, Office Action at 2-3. Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection for at least the following reasons.

The Office fails to properly identify the alleged abstract idea: On January 7, 2019, the USPTO released revised guidance for evaluating subject matter eligibility. 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, 84 Fed. Reg. 50 (Jan. 7, 2019) (hereinafter "2019 PEG"). Additionally, the USPTO released an update to the 2019 PEG on October 17, 2019. October 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance Update, available at https://www.uspto.gov/ patent/laws-and- regulations/examination-policy/subject-matter-eligibility (hereinafter "October 2019 Update").
For example, the 2019 PEG explains:
"[T]he abstract idea exception includes the following groupings of subject matter, when recited as such in a claim
limitation(s) (that is, when recited on their own or per se):
(a) Mathematical concepts-mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, mathematical calculations;

(b) Certain methods of organizing human activity fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); commercial or legal interactions (including agreements in the form of contracts; legal obligations; advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors; business relations); managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities, teaching, and
following rules or instructions); and
(c) Mental processes concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion)."
2019 PEG at 52.

MPEP 2106.04(a) states that "Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by...determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above." Here, the Office fails identify any grouping into which the alleged abstract idea falls.

Further, the 2019 PEG explains that "[c]laims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas," except in "rare" circumstances. See 2019 PEG at 53. Initially, Applicant notes that the characterization of the claims is an oversimplification and the claims do not recite an exception. The MPEP states that "Examiners should ... be careful to distinguish claims that recite an exception (which require further eligibility analysis) and claims that merely involve an exception (which are eligible and do not require further eligibility analysis)." MPEP § 2106.04(II)(A)(1) (emphasis in original). In particular, the assertion that the claims are directed to "processing data according to the rules of a game," "displaying the output," and "accepting input," mischaracterizes the nature of the claims and leads to the erroneous conclusion that the claims recite an exception. The claims, when taken as a whole, recite steps that include a technical solution to computer-centric problem, namely increasing efficient use of computing resources. That is, rather than merely "processing data according to the rules of a game," "displaying the output," and "accepting input," the claims ensure that "computing resources are saved and optimally used" "since real-time positions of the virtual props need not be calculated for a long time." See, Specification at [0018], [0117]. And further, "because an operation process of triggering the first virtual prop is relatively simple, the man- machine interaction efficiency also improves." See, Specification at [0018].

Nevertheless, even if amended claim 1 is treated as reciting a judicial exception (which Applicant does not concede), it recites features that, when considered as a whole, integrate any such exception into a practical application and thus render the claim eligible. In particular, and as explained in the 2019 PEG, under the revised procedure for evaluating subject matter eligibility:

"[I]f a claim recites a judicial exception (a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea as grouped in Section I, above), it must then be analyzed to determine whether the recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application of that exception.
A claim is not "directed to" a judicial exception and thus is patent

eligible, if the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of that exception. A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception." 2019 PEG at 53.

Thus, even if claim 1 were treated as reciting a judicial exception, the specific series of computer-executed instructions recited in independent claim 1 applies and uses any such "judicial exception in a specific manner, thereby imposing a meaningful limit on the scope of independent claim 1, such that claim 1 amounts to more than a drafting effort to monopolize any such judicial exception. For example, claim 1 recites: displaying a first user interface (UI), the first UI comprising a first virtual environment image, the first virtual environment image corresponding to an image of a virtual environment observed
from a perspective of a first virtual character,

controlling, in response to a use instruction for a first virtual prop, the first virtual character to use the first virtual prop, the first virtual prop being a virtual prop used for generating a defense range, the defense range being a range in which the first virtual prop is capable of producing a defense effect against an attack from a second virtual prop, the second virtual prop having a function of
chasing a target virtual character; and
intercepting the second virtual prop based on determining that the second virtual prop will fall within the defense range.

The recited features are directed to a specific application in which a first virtual prop is provided specifically for intercepting other virtual props within a defense range, thus eliminating the need to compute real-time positions of the virtual props for a long time and saving and optimally using computing resources. Thus, claim 1 integrates any such judicial exception into a practical application and therefore is eligible. See 2019 PEG at 54 ("If the recited exception is integrated into a practical application of the exception, then the claim is eligible at Prong Two of revised Step 2A. This concludes the eligibility analysis.").
This conclusion is even more apparent when considered in view of the October 2019 Update. In particular, the October 2019 Update explains that:

"[T]he Prong Two analysis considers the claim as a whole. That is, the limitations containing the judicial exception as well as the additional elements in the claim besides the judicial exception need to be evaluated together to determine whether the claim integrates thejudicial exception into a practical applicati SVG {EMBED HERE} 0.2671.34 limitations should not be evaluated in a vacuum, from the recited judicial exception. Instead, the analysis should take into consideration all the claim limitations and how those limitations interact and impact each other when evaluating whether the exception is integrated into a practical application. For example in Bascom Global Internet Servs., Inc. v. AT&T Mobility LLC, the court determined the claim recited the abstract idea of"filtering." However, it concluded the claimed invention improved technology because the filtering tool was installed at a specific location, remote from the end- users, with customizable filtering features specific to each end user which provided both the benefits of a filter at a local computer and on an ISP server. In determining whether the claimed invention improves technology, the court considered the filtering limitations in
combination with the remaining limitations." October 2019 Update at 12 (emphasis added).

Here, when taking into consideration all the claim limitations and how those limitations interact and impact each other when evaluating whether the exception is integrated into a practical application, as mandated by the October 2019 Update, one may conclude that the claimed invention improves technology because it ensures the efficient and optimal use of computing resources by eliminating the need for a computer to perform certain real-time computations.

Even if the claim is not patent eligible at Step 2A, which Applicant does not concede, further analysis is still required at Step 2B. See 2019 Guidance at 16; see also 22-24. "Evaluating additional elements to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure that they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself." MPEP 2106.05. Nothing in the cited portion of Applicant's specification, or the specification in general, constitutes an "express statement" that the elements are well- understood, routine and conventional, as required.

Furthermore, the rejection of the claims does not support the conclusion that the actual language of the claims, or the claims as a whole, recite a "combination of elements [that represent] well-understood, routine, conventional activity [.. .] widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry." MPEP 2106.05. According to the MPEP, "[e]ven if one or more additional
elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity when considered individually, the combination of additional elements may amount to an inventive concept." MPEP 2106.05(d).

Further, even assuming, without conceding, that the claims are directed to "processing data according to the rules of a game," "displaying the output," and "accepting input," as asserted by the Office Action, clearly aspects of the claims directed to improving the efficient and optimal use of computing resources constitute significantly more than merely "processing data according to the rules of a game," "displaying the output," and "accepting input."
For at least these reasons, Applicant submits that claim 1 is directed to patent-eligible subject matter.

Claims 10 and 19 recite similar, though not identical, features to those recited in claim 1. For at least similar reasons as those described above with regard to claim 1, claims 15 and 19 recite patent eligible subject matter. Claims 2-9, 11-18, and 20 depend from one of claims 1, 10, or 19. At least by virtue of their dependence on an allowable independent claim, claims 2-9, 11-18, and 20 also recite patent eligible subject matter.
In view of the foregoing, withdrawal of the rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 101 is respectfully requested.

Claims 1-20 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) as allegedly being unpatentable over Chinese Patent Publication No. 110613938 (hereinafter "Liu") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2007/0243914 (hereinafter "Yan").
Applicant traverses these rejections.
Claim 1 recites:
controlling, in response to a use instruction for a first virtual prop,

the first virtual character to use the first virtual prop, the first virtual prop being a virtual prop used for generating a defense range, the defense range being a range in which the first virtual prop is capable of producing a defense effect against an attack from a second virtual prop.

The Office rejects this feature in view of [43]-[46] of Tencent '938, which allegedly teaches "plac[ing] a virtual auto-attack prop 106 in a suitable area in the virtual environment" wherein "the virtual auto-attack prop 106 can automatically attack a target object within an attack range." See, Office Action at 13. The Office contends that the claimed "first virtual prop" corresponds to Tencent '938's "virtual auto-attack prop 106." But per the Office's own characterization, the virtual auto-attack prop 106 "can automatically attack a target object within an attack range." In contrast, claim 1 recites "the first virtual prop being a virtual prop used for generating a defense range, the defense range being a range in which the first virtual prop is capable of producing a defense effect against an attack from a second virtual prop." Thus, the claimed "first virtual prop" does not correspond the Tencent '938's "virtual auto-attack prop 106" as characterized by the Office.
Claim 1 further recites:
the second virtual prop having a function of chasing a target virtual character.

The Office contends that this feature is taught by [24] of Yan, and specifically, by Yan allegedly teaching that "opponent virtual weapon b22 of host toy device 2 is able to 'destroy' host toy device 1 [and virtual weapon b 1] when it is in range." See, Office Action 15. But even assuming, without conceding, that Yan's virtual weapon bl 1 (the alleged "second virtual prop") is destroyed by virtual weapon b22, Yan still does not teach or suggest that virtual weapon b 11 "[has] a function of chasing a target virtual character," as recited in claim 1.
Thus Tencent '938 and Yan, considered alone or in combination, fail to teach or suggest at least the above-recited features of claim 1.

Claims 10 and 19 recite similar, though not identical, features to those recited in claim 1. For at least similar reasons as those described above with regard to claim 1, claims 15 and 19 are allowable over Tencent '938 and Yan. Claims 2-9, 11-18, and 20 depend from one of claims 1, 10, or 19. At least by virtue of their dependence on an allowable independent claim, claims 2-9, 11-18, and 20 are also allowable over Tencent '938 and Yan.

Based on the foregoing, Applicant respectfully submits that the application is in condition for allowance and a Notice to that effect is earnestly solicited. Should the Examiner believe that anything further is desirable in order to place the application in even better form for allowance, the Examiner is invited to contact Applicant's undersigned representative at the below-listed number.
Respectfully submitted, BANNER & WITCOFF, LTD.
